```{r clt-settings}
n_small <- 5      # "small" sample size
n_large <- 50     # "large" sample size
N       <- 20000  # number of simulated samples for each (population, n)
```
```{r populations}
pops <- list(
  # ---- continuous ----
  Normal = list(label = "Normal(0, 1)", discrete = FALSE,
                draw = function(m) rnorm(m), mu = 0, sigma = 1,
                dens = function(x) dnorm(x), xlim = c(-4, 4)),
  Uniform = list(label = "Uniform(0, 1)", discrete = FALSE,
                 draw = function(m) runif(m), mu = 0.5, sigma = sqrt(1/12),
                 dens = function(x) dunif(x), xlim = c(-0.2, 1.2)),
  Exponential = list(label = "Exponential (mean 1), right-skewed", discrete = FALSE,
                     draw = function(m) rexp(m, 1), mu = 1, sigma = 1,
                     dens = function(x) dexp(x, 1), xlim = c(0, 5)),
  Bimodal = list(label = "Two-humped (50/50 mix of N(-1.5, 0.5^2), N(1.5, 0.5^2))",
                 discrete = FALSE,
                 draw = function(m) ifelse(runif(m) < 0.5, rnorm(m, -1.5, 0.5), rnorm(m, 1.5, 0.5)),
                 mu = 0, sigma = sqrt(0.25 + 1.5^2),
                 dens = function(x) 0.5 * dnorm(x, -1.5, 0.5) + 0.5 * dnorm(x, 1.5, 0.5),
                 xlim = c(-4, 4)),
  # ---- discrete (integer valued) ----
  Die = list(label = "Fair die (discrete uniform on 1..6)", discrete = TRUE,
             draw = function(m) sample(1:6, m, replace = TRUE),
             mu = 3.5, sigma = sqrt(35/12), support = 1:6, pmf = rep(1/6, 6)),
  Bernoulli = list(label = "Bernoulli(p = 0.1), very skewed", discrete = TRUE,
                   draw = function(m) rbinom(m, 1, 0.1),
                   mu = 0.1, sigma = sqrt(0.1 * 0.9), support = 0:1, pmf = c(0.9, 0.1))
)

col_bar   <- "#dbe8f5"   # light blue : bars / histogram
col_event <- "#7fb5dc"   # blue       : bars that belong to the event
col_curve <- "#cb181d"   # red        : normal curve
col_shade <- adjustcolor("#fd8d3c", alpha.f = 0.38)  # orange: normal area
```
```{r clt-functions}
# draw m*n values and return the m sample means
sim_means <- function(pop, n, m = N) rowMeans(matrix(pop$draw(m * n), nrow = m, ncol = n))

plot_population <- function(pop) {
  if (pop$discrete) {
    plot(pop$support, pop$pmf, type = "h", lwd = 8, lend = 1, col = col_event,
         xlim = range(pop$support) + c(-0.8, 0.8), ylim = c(0, max(pop$pmf) * 1.15),
         xlab = "x", ylab = "probability",
         main = paste0("Population\n", pop$label), cex.main = 0.85)
  } else {
    xs <- seq(pop$xlim[1], pop$xlim[2], length.out = 600)
    plot(xs, pop$dens(xs), type = "n", xlab = "x", ylab = "density",
         ylim = c(0, max(pop$dens(xs)) * 1.1),
         main = paste0("Population\n", pop$label), cex.main = 0.85)
    polygon(c(xs[1], xs, xs[length(xs)]), c(0, pop$dens(xs), 0), col = col_bar, border = col_event, lwd = 2)
  }
}

plot_xbar <- function(pop, n, m = N, main = NULL) {
  xbar <- sim_means(pop, n, m)
  se   <- pop$sigma / sqrt(n)
  xl   <- pop$mu + c(-4, 4) * se
  xs   <- seq(xl[1], xl[2], length.out = 500)
  if (is.null(main))
    main <- sprintf("Sample mean, n = %d\nmean = %.2f, SD = %.3f", n, pop$mu, se)

  if (pop$discrete) {                       # sums are integers: area of each bar = P(Xbar = v)
    tab <- table(round(xbar * n)) / m
    v   <- as.numeric(names(tab)) / n
    h   <- as.numeric(tab) * n              # probability / bar width (width = 1/n)
    ymax <- max(h, dnorm(pop$mu, pop$mu, se)) * 1.15
    plot(NA, xlim = xl, ylim = c(0, ymax), xlab = "sample mean", ylab = "density",
         main = main, cex.main = 0.85)
    rect(v - 0.5 / n, 0, v + 0.5 / n, h, col = col_bar, border = "white")
  } else {
    br   <- seq(xl[1], xl[2], length.out = 41)
    keep <- xbar[xbar >= xl[1] & xbar <= xl[2]]
    cnt  <- hist(keep, breaks = br, plot = FALSE)$counts
    h    <- cnt / (m * diff(br))            # density scale (uses all m samples)
    ymax <- max(h, dnorm(pop$mu, pop$mu, se)) * 1.15
    plot(NA, xlim = xl, ylim = c(0, ymax), xlab = "sample mean", ylab = "density",
         main = main, cex.main = 0.85)
    rect(br[-length(br)], 0, br[-1], h, col = col_bar, border = "white")
  }
  lines(xs, dnorm(xs, pop$mu, se), col = col_curve, lwd = 2.5)
}

# one row per population: [population | small n | large n]
clt_grid <- function(pop_names, n_small, n_large) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(length(pop_names), 3), mar = c(4, 4, 3.6, 1))
  on.exit(par(op))
  for (nm in pop_names) {
    plot_population(pops[[nm]])
    plot_xbar(pops[[nm]], n_small)
    plot_xbar(pops[[nm]], n_large)
  }
}
```
```{r cc-functions}
# distribution "families": pmf, mean, sd, largest value worth considering
fam_binom <- function(n, p) list(name = sprintf("Bin(%d, %g)", n, p), pmf = function(x) dbinom(x, n, p),
                                 mu = n * p, sigma = sqrt(n * p * (1 - p)), maxx = n)
fam_pois  <- function(lambda) list(name = sprintf("Poisson(%g)", lambda), pmf = function(x) dpois(x, lambda),
                                   mu = lambda, sigma = sqrt(lambda), maxx = qpois(1 - 1e-12, lambda))

# event P(X <= k), etc.: which integers belong to it, and the matching normal interval
event_info <- function(kind, k) {
  op  <- c(le = "<=", lt = "<", ge = ">=", gt = ">", eq = "==")[[kind]]
  sym <- c(le = "<=", lt = "<", ge = ">=", gt = ">", eq = "=")[[kind]]
  list(inc  = switch(kind, le = function(v) v <= k, lt = function(v) v < k, ge = function(v) v >= k,
                           gt = function(v) v > k,  eq = function(v) v == k),
       lab     = call("paste", "P(", call(op, quote(X), k), ")"),      # plotmath label, used in plot titles
       lab_chr = sprintf("P(X %s %d)", sym, k),         # text label, used in tables
       cc   = switch(kind, le = c(-Inf, k + 0.5), lt = c(-Inf, k - 0.5), ge = c(k - 0.5, Inf),
                           gt = c(k + 0.5, Inf),  eq = c(k - 0.5, k + 0.5)),
       nocc = switch(kind, le = c(-Inf, k), lt = c(-Inf, k), ge = c(k, Inf), gt = c(k, Inf), eq = c(k, k)))
}

# one panel. mode = "exact" (bars only), "nocc" (normal area, no correction), "cc" (normal area, corrected)
panel <- function(fam, k, kind = "le", mode = c("exact", "nocc", "cc"), xlim = NULL) {
  mode <- match.arg(mode)
  ev   <- event_info(kind, k)
  if (is.null(xlim)) xlim <- fam$mu + c(-3.5, 3.5) * fam$sigma
  v <- max(0, floor(xlim[1])):min(fam$maxx, ceiling(xlim[2]))
  p <- fam$pmf(v)
  allv  <- 0:fam$maxx
  exact <- sum(fam$pmf(allv)[ev$inc(allv)])

  reg    <- if (mode == "cc") ev$cc else ev$nocc
  approx <- if (reg[1] < reg[2]) pnorm(reg[2], fam$mu, fam$sigma) - pnorm(reg[1], fam$mu, fam$sigma) else 0
  fin    <- unique(reg[is.finite(reg)])

  line1 <- if (mode == "exact") "Exact: area of the bars" else {
    where <- if (length(fin) == 1 && reg[1] == reg[2]) sprintf("at x = %g (zero width)", fin) else
             sprintf("boundary %s", paste(fin, collapse = " and "))
    sprintf("Normal area, %s", where)
  }
  line2 <- if (mode == "exact") bquote(.(ev$lab) == .(sprintf("%.4f", exact))) else
           bquote(.(ev$lab) %~~% .(sprintf("%.4f", approx)) * "   (error " * .(sprintf("%+.4f", approx - exact)) * ")")

  ymax <- max(p, if (mode != "exact") dnorm(fam$mu, fam$mu, fam$sigma)) * 1.15
  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0, ymax), xlab = "x", ylab = "probability / density", main = "")
  title(main = line1, cex.main = 0.85, line = 2.1)
  mtext(line2, side = 3, line = 0.8, font = 2, cex = 0.85)

  # bars: blue = belongs to the event
  rect(v - 0.5, 0, v + 0.5, p, col = ifelse(ev$inc(v), col_event, col_bar),
       border = if (length(v) > 40) NA else "white")
  # the pmf as a step function
  lines(c(rbind(v - 0.5, v + 0.5)), rep(p, each = 2), col = "grey25", lwd = 1.3)

  if (mode != "exact") {
    lo <- max(reg[1], xlim[1]); hi <- min(reg[2], xlim[2])
    if (lo < hi) {
      xs <- seq(lo, hi, length.out = 300)
      polygon(c(lo, xs, hi), c(0, dnorm(xs, fam$mu, fam$sigma), 0), col = col_shade, border = NA)
    }
    xs <- seq(xlim[1], xlim[2], length.out = 500)
    lines(xs, dnorm(xs, fam$mu, fam$sigma), col = col_curve, lwd = 2.5)
    abline(v = fin, lty = 2, lwd = 1.5)
  }
  invisible(c(exact = exact, approx = approx))
}

# exact / no correction / with correction side by side
three_panels <- function(fam, k, kind = "le", xlim = NULL) {
  op <- par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 4, 1)); par(cex = 1); on.exit(par(op))
  panel(fam, k, kind, "exact", xlim)
  panel(fam, k, kind, "nocc",  xlim)
  panel(fam, k, kind, "cc",    xlim)
}

# numbers for all five event types
cc_table <- function(fam, k) {
  kinds <- c("eq", "lt", "le", "ge", "gt")
  out <- t(sapply(kinds, function(kd) {
    pdf(NULL); on.exit(dev.off())
    c(exact = panel(fam, k, kd, "exact")[["exact"]],
      nocc  = panel(fam, k, kd, "nocc")[["approx"]],
      cc    = panel(fam, k, kd, "cc")[["approx"]])
  }))
  data.frame(Event = sapply(kinds, function(kd) event_info(kd, k)$lab_chr),
             `Normal interval used` = sapply(kinds, function(kd) {
               r <- event_info(kd, k)$cc
               if (is.infinite(r[1])) sprintf("X* < %g", r[2]) else if (is.infinite(r[2])) sprintf("X* > %g", r[1])
               else sprintf("%g < X* < %g", r[1], r[2]) }),
             Exact = round(out[, "exact"], 4),
             `No correction` = round(out[, "nocc"], 4),
             `With correction` = round(out[, "cc"], 4),
             check.names = FALSE, row.names = NULL)
}
```

```{r by-hand-helper}
# "by hand" table: z-score(s), z-table value (z rounded to 2 decimals), and software value
by_hand <- function(fam, k, kind = "le") {
  ev <- event_info(kind, k)
  one <- function(reg, method) {
    fin  <- reg[is.finite(reg)]
    zr   <- round((reg - fam$mu) / fam$sigma, 2)
    nonempty <- reg[1] < reg[2]
    tab  <- if (nonempty) round(pnorm(zr[2]), 4) - round(pnorm(zr[1]), 4) else 0   # 4-decimal table entries
    soft <- if (nonempty) pnorm(reg[2], fam$mu, fam$sigma) - pnorm(reg[1], fam$mu, fam$sigma) else 0
    data.frame(Method = method,
               `Normal boundary` = if (nonempty) paste(fin, collapse = " and ") else sprintf("%g (zero width)", fin[1]),
               `z-score` = if (nonempty) paste(sprintf("%.2f", zr[is.finite(zr)]), collapse = " and ") else "-",
               `From z-table` = sprintf("%.4f", tab), `From software` = sprintf("%.4f", soft),
               check.names = FALSE)
  }
  allv <- 0:fam$maxx
  ex <- sum(fam$pmf(allv)[ev$inc(allv)])
  rbind(one(ev$nocc, "Normal, no correction"), one(ev$cc, "Normal, with correction"),
        data.frame(Method = "Exact (pmf)", `Normal boundary` = "-", `z-score` = "-",
                   `From z-table` = "-", `From software` = sprintf("%.4f", ex), check.names = FALSE))
}
```

This document has two parts.

* **Part 1** shows what the Central Limit Theorem (CLT) says about the distribution of the sample mean $\bar X$ for different populations and sample sizes.
* **Part 2** shows why a **continuity correction** is needed when a discrete distribution (Binomial or Poisson) is approximated by a normal distribution.

# Part 1. Central Limit Theorem: what does the distribution of $\bar X$ look like?

**CLT.** Let $X_1, \dots, X_n$ be a random sample (i.i.d.) from a population with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$. Then $E[\bar X] = \mu$ and $SD(\bar X) = \sigma/\sqrt n$, and for large $n$

$$\bar X \approx N\left(\mu,\ \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).$$

If the population itself is normal, this is exact for every $n$. If the population is not normal and $n$ is small, the approximation can be poor. The pictures below show how this plays out.

**How to read the pictures.**

* Each row is one population. The **left** panel is the population distribution itself. The **middle** and **right** panels are the distribution of the sample mean for $n = `r n_small`$ and $n = `r n_large`$.
* For each population and each $n$, we generated `r format(N, big.mark = ",")` random samples of size $n$, computed $\bar X$ for each sample, and drew a histogram of those `r format(N, big.mark = ",")` sample means (on the density scale). The histograms are random, so they wobble a little around the true shape.
* The **red curve** is the CLT approximation, the normal pdf with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt n$. If the histogram follows the red curve, the CLT approximation is good.
* For a **discrete** population, $\bar X$ can only take the values $0, 1/n, 2/n, \dots$, so the histogram is a set of bars of width $1/n$ whose **area** equals $P(\bar X = v)$. This puts it on the same scale as the red pdf.
* The horizontal axis of each sample-mean panel is zoomed to $\mu \pm 4$ standard deviations of $\bar X$. The panels at larger $n$ therefore look about as wide as the ones at smaller $n$. To see the spread shrinking, read the axis numbers and the SD printed in each panel title.

## Continuous populations

```{r clt-continuous, fig.width=11, fig.height=12}
clt_grid(c("Normal", "Uniform", "Exponential", "Bimodal"), n_small, n_large)
```

**What to notice**

* *Normal population:* $\bar X$ is exactly normal for **any** $n$. The red curve fits already at $n = `r n_small`$; only the spread shrinks.
* *Uniform population (symmetric):* $\bar X$ is already close to normal at $n = `r n_small`$.
* *Exponential population (skewed):* at $n = `r n_small`$ the histogram is still skewed, and the normal curve even puts some area below 0 although the population cannot be negative. At $n = `r n_large`$ the fit is good, but not perfect.
* *Two-humped population:* the sample mean is a single hump even though the population has two. Averaging smooths out the shape.
* In every row the center stays at $\mu$ and the spread shrinks like $\sigma/\sqrt n$. Look at the "SD" in the panel titles.

## Discrete populations

```{r clt-discrete, fig.width=11, fig.height=6}
clt_grid(c("Die", "Bernoulli"), n_small, n_large)
```

**What to notice**

* Even for a discrete population, $\bar X$ becomes bell shaped. The bars are on a grid of spacing $1/n$, which is finer for larger $n$.
* The die is symmetric, so the fit is good quickly. The Bernoulli(0.1) population is very skewed, and at $n = 50$ ($np = 5$) the bars are still visibly lopsided. This matches the rule of thumb $np \ge 5$ and $n(1-p) \ge 5$ as the **minimum**.
* Because the exact distribution is a set of bars while the red curve is smooth, a continuity correction is needed whenever we compute probabilities. That is Part 2.

## Watching the shape change as $n$ grows

For the two most skewed populations, we increase $n$ step by step. Top row: Exponential (continuous). Bottom row: Bernoulli(0.1) (discrete). For $n = 1$ the "sample mean" is a single observation, so that panel is just the population.

```{r clt-progression, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
ns <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 30, 100)
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, length(ns)), mar = c(4, 4, 3.6, 1))
for (nm in c("Exponential", "Bernoulli"))
  for (n in ns)
    plot_xbar(pops[[nm]], n,
              main = sprintf("%s, n = %d\nSD = %.3f", nm, n, pops[[nm]]$sigma / sqrt(n)))
par(op)
```

**What to notice.** The skewness fades gradually as $n$ grows, and the histogram settles onto the red curve. The Exponential row looks close to normal by about $n = 30$. The Bernoulli(0.1) row needs a larger $n$, because the population is more extreme. The spread of $\bar X$ (printed as SD in each title) keeps shrinking like $1/\sqrt n$.

## How good is the CLT approximation? (exact vs. approximate numbers)

For the Exponential(mean 1) population, the sum of $n$ observations is exactly Gamma($n$, rate 1), so we can compute an upper-tail probability exactly and compare it with the CLT answer. We use the cutoff $\mu + 1.645\,\sigma/\sqrt n$, for which the CLT answer is always $P(Z > 1.645) \approx 0.05$.

```{r clt-table}
n_vals <- c(5, 10, 30, 50, 100, 200, 500)
cutoff <- 1 + 1.645 / sqrt(n_vals)                       # mu + 1.645 * sigma / sqrt(n)
exact  <- pgamma(n_vals * cutoff, shape = n_vals, rate = 1, lower.tail = FALSE)
clt    <- pnorm(cutoff, mean = 1, sd = 1 / sqrt(n_vals), lower.tail = FALSE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(n = n_vals, Cutoff = round(cutoff, 3), `Exact` = round(exact, 4),
                        `CLT (normal)` = round(clt, 4), `Difference` = round(clt - exact, 4),
                        check.names = FALSE),
             caption = "P(sample mean > cutoff) for the Exponential(mean 1) population")
```

"Difference" is (CLT value $-$ exact value). The exact tail probability is larger than 0.05 for small $n$ because of the right skew, and it approaches the CLT value of 0.05 only slowly as $n$ grows.

------------------------------------------------------------------------

# Part 2. Continuity correction

**Setup.** A discrete $X$ (Binomial or Poisson) is approximated by a continuous $X^* \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ with the same mean and variance.

**Key picture.** Draw the pmf as a **step function**: over each integer $v$, a bar of width 1 centered at $v$ and height $P(X = v)$. Because the width is 1, **area of the bar = $P(X = v)$**. The bar for $v$ covers the interval $(v - 0.5,\ v + 0.5)$. So the exact probability is an area made of whole bars, and the normal approximation should be an area measured against the same bars.


**How to read the pictures.**

* **Light blue bars:** the exact pmf of $X$. Each bar has width 1 and is centered at an integer.
* **Dark blue bars:** the values of $X$ that belong to the event we are computing.
* **Black outline:** the same pmf drawn as a step function.
* **Red curve:** the pdf of the approximating normal $X^*$.
* **Orange shading:** the normal area used for the approximation. It is semi-transparent, so the bars show through.
* **Dashed vertical line(s):** where the normal area starts or stops.
* **Error** in a panel title means (approximation $-$ exact).

## Example 1: $X \sim \text{Bin}(20,\ 0.3)$

Here $np = 6 \ge 5$ and $n(1-p) = 14 \ge 5$, so the normal approximation is allowed, with $X^* \sim N(6,\ 4.2)$. We approximate $P(X \le 6)$. For a Binomial, the rule from class is

$$P(X \le k) \approx \Phi\left(\frac{k + 0.5 - np}{\sqrt{np(1-p)}}\right).$$

First, the objects involved: the pmf as bars (and as a step function) and the normal pdf on top.

```{r cc-overview, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
fam <- fam_binom(20, 0.3)
v <- 0:14
plot(NA, xlim = c(-0.5, 14.5), ylim = c(0, 0.2), xlab = "x", ylab = "probability / density",
     main = "Bin(20, 0.3): bars = pmf, red = N(6, 4.2) pdf")
rect(v - 0.5, 0, v + 0.5, fam$pmf(v), col = col_bar, border = "white")
lines(c(rbind(v - 0.5, v + 0.5)), rep(fam$pmf(v), each = 2), col = "grey25", lwd = 1.3)
xs <- seq(-0.5, 14.5, length.out = 400)
lines(xs, dnorm(xs, fam$mu, fam$sigma), col = col_curve, lwd = 2.5)
```

### $P(X \le 6)$: three ways to measure the area

* **Left:** the exact probability is the total area of the blue bars for $x = 0, \dots, 6$. This area stops at the **right edge of the bar for 6, which is 6.5**.
* **Middle:** without the correction we measure the normal area up to 6. That cuts the bar for 6 in half, so half a bar is lost.
* **Right:** with the correction we measure the normal area up to 6.5. This lines up with the right edge of the bar.

```{r cc-le, fig.width=13, fig.height=4.5}
three_panels(fam, k = 6, kind = "le")
```

**By hand.** $X^* \sim N(6,\ 4.2)$, so $\sigma = \sqrt{4.2} \approx 2.05$ and $z = (x - 6)/2.05$.

```{r cc-le-hand}
knitr::kable(by_hand(fam, 6, "le"), caption = "Bin(20, 0.3): P(X <= 6)")
```

Without the correction we get $\Phi(0) = 0.5000$, which is far below the exact $0.6080$. With the correction, $P(X^* < 6.5) = \Phi\left(\frac{6.5 - 6}{2.05}\right) = \Phi(0.24) = 0.5948$ (z-table) or $0.5964$ (software). Both are close to the exact value.

### $P(X = 6)$: why the correction is necessary

Without the correction, $P(X^* = 6) = 0$ for a continuous variable, which is useless. The bar for 6 has width 1, so we measure the normal area over the same interval, $(5.5,\ 6.5)$.

```{r cc-eq, fig.width=13, fig.height=4.5}
three_panels(fam, k = 6, kind = "eq", xlim = c(1.5, 10.5))
```

```{r cc-eq-hand}
knitr::kable(by_hand(fam, 6, "eq"), caption = "Bin(20, 0.3): P(X = 6)")
```

With the correction, $P(5.5 < X^* < 6.5) = \Phi(0.24) - \Phi(-0.24) = 0.5948 - 0.4052 = 0.1896$ (z-table) or $0.1927$ (software), compared with the exact $0.1916$.

### Which boundary to use for each inequality

The rule is: **move the boundary to the edge of the bar so that the bar for $k$ is included or excluded exactly as the inequality says.**

```{r cc-four, fig.width=11, fig.height=8}
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 4, 1))
for (kd in c("lt", "le", "ge", "gt")) panel(fam, 5, kd, "cc")
par(op)
```

```{r cc-rules-table}
knitr::kable(cc_table(fam, k = 5), caption = "Bin(20, 0.3), k = 5: exact vs. normal approximation")
```

In this table, "Normal interval used" is the interval for $X^*$ after the correction. The "No correction" column is clearly off, and the "With correction" column is close to the exact values for all five events.

### Does the correction still matter when $n$ is large?

We compare the error of the two methods for $P(X \le np)$ with $p = 0.3$.

```{r cc-error, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
n_seq <- c(10, 20, 50, 100, 200, 500, 1000)
p0 <- 0.3
err <- sapply(n_seq, function(n) {
  k  <- floor(n * p0)
  ex <- pbinom(k, n, p0)
  s  <- sqrt(n * p0 * (1 - p0))
  c(nocc = abs(pnorm(k, n * p0, s) - ex), cc = abs(pnorm(k + 0.5, n * p0, s) - ex))
})
matplot(n_seq, t(err), type = "b", pch = 16, lty = 1, lwd = 2, col = c("grey40", col_curve),
        log = "xy", xlab = "n (log scale)", ylab = "absolute error (log scale)",
        main = expression("Error of the normal approximation to " * P(X <= np) * ", p = 0.3"))
legend("topright", c("no correction", "with continuity correction"), col = c("grey40", col_curve),
       lty = 1, pch = 16, lwd = 2, bty = "n")
```

The vertical axis is the absolute difference between the approximation and the exact probability, on a log scale. Both errors shrink as $n$ grows, but the corrected version is more accurate at every $n$ shown.

## Example 2 (preview for next class): $X \sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda)$

The idea is identical. The bars are the Poisson pmf, and $X^* \sim N(\lambda, \lambda)$. The rule of thumb is $\lambda > 10$, and

$$P(X \le k) \approx \Phi\left(\frac{k + 0.5 - \lambda}{\sqrt{\lambda}}\right).$$

### $\lambda = 12$: approximate $P(X \le 9)$

```{r cc-pois12, fig.width=13, fig.height=4.5}
three_panels(fam_pois(12), k = 9, kind = "le")
```

```{r cc-pois12-hand}
knitr::kable(by_hand(fam_pois(12), 9, "le"), caption = "Poisson(12): P(X <= 9), with X* ~ N(12, 12), sigma = 3.46")
```

### A case where the approximation is poor: $\lambda = 3$

The Poisson(3) pmf is skewed and the normal curve even puts area below 0, so even the corrected answer is noticeably off. This is why we require $\lambda$ to be large.

```{r cc-pois3, fig.width=13, fig.height=4.5}
three_panels(fam_pois(3), k = 2, kind = "le", xlim = c(-3, 10))
```

```{r cc-pois3-hand}
knitr::kable(by_hand(fam_pois(3), 2, "le"), caption = "Poisson(3): P(X <= 2), with X* ~ N(3, 3), sigma = 1.73")
```

### A realistic case: $\lambda = 219$, $P(X \le 200)$

This is the setting of the power-plant accident question (0.6 accidents per day for 365 days). The bars are very thin at this scale, so all three panels look alike, but the half-bar still changes the answer in the third decimal place. Here are the numbers:

```{r cc-pois219, fig.width=13, fig.height=4.5}
three_panels(fam_pois(219), k = 200, kind = "le", xlim = c(180, 215))
```

```{r cc-pois219-hand}
knitr::kable(by_hand(fam_pois(219), 200, "le"), caption = "Poisson(219): P(X <= 200), with X* ~ N(219, 219), sigma = 14.80")
```

With the correction, $P(X \le 200) \approx \Phi\left(\frac{200.5 - 219}{\sqrt{219}}\right) = \Phi(-1.25) = 0.1056$ by the z-table.

```{r cc-pois219-table}
knitr::kable(cc_table(fam_pois(219), k = 200), caption = "Poisson(219), k = 200")
```

**Summary of the rule** (same for Binomial and Poisson, for integer $k$):

| Exact probability | Approximate with $X^*$ |
|:--|:--|
| $P(X = k)$ | $P(k - 0.5 < X^* < k + 0.5)$ |
| $P(X \le k)$ | $P(X^* < k + 0.5)$ |
| $P(X < k)$ | $P(X^* < k - 0.5)$ |
| $P(X \ge k)$ | $P(X^* > k - 0.5)$ |
| $P(X > k)$ | $P(X^* > k + 0.5)$ |
